source.title: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises?
source.summary: Big moments from headline acts are shared online long before many fans see their favourite artists.
source.evidence_text:
Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises?
Big moments from headline acts are shared online long before many fans see their favourite artists.
You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view.
While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise.
Aurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul".
Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them.
Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected.
Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.
But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.
Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.
"One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."
Phoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether.
It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise".
But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted".
"When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says.
"I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get."
McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing.
"Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds.
Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run.
"If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."
Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out.
McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans.
But Collins says she's "not totally against it".
What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want.
But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds.
"I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script.

vocabulary.definition: to ruin something good, often by telling a secret or making it less fun
a live music show, usually with one or more singers or bands
on the internet, using a computer or phone to see information
special, short times or parts of an event
to keep away from something or someone; to prevent something from happening

grammar.explanation: We use 'can' to talk about things that are possible or things that are able to happen. It shows that something might happen or is allowed to happen.

quiz.question: What problem does social media sometimes create for concert fans?
options: It makes tickets more expensive.
It spoils surprises for shows.
It stops artists from performing.
option_feedback: The text does not say ticket prices go up because of social media.
Yes, social media can show big moments before fans see them live.
The text says artists still perform, but their shows might be spoiled.

quiz.question: What do some fans do to keep concert surprises?
options: They buy special tickets.
They watch more online videos.
They try to avoid online spoilers.
option_feedback: The text does not mention special tickets for avoiding spoilers.
Watching more videos would show them more spoilers, not keep surprises.
Correct! Some fans, like Aurélia Collins, try to avoid online videos to stay surprised.

quiz.question: What does the word 'spoil' mean in the sentence 'Social media can sometimes spoil big concert surprises'?
options: to make something better
to ruin something good
to buy something new
option_feedback: 'Spoil' means the opposite of making something better in this context.
Exactly! To 'spoil' a surprise means to ruin it or make it less special.
Buying something new is not related to the meaning of 'spoil' here.

quiz.question: Which sentence from the text uses 'can' to show that something is possible?
options: 'Many people see special moments from concerts online...'
'Social media can sometimes spoil big concert surprises...'
'But other fans like to know everything before they attend a show.'
option_feedback: This sentence tells us what people do, not what is possible.
Correct. 'Can' shows that it is possible for social media to spoil surprises.
This sentence describes what some fans like, not a possibility.

quiz.question: How do some artists try to give fans new surprises during their shows?
options: They stop all online videos.
They change their shows a little each night.
They only play new songs.
option_feedback: The text mentions banning phones at some shows, but not stopping all online videos generally.
That's right! Artists might change songs or stage designs to keep things fresh.
The text says they change their shows, not that they only play new songs.

quiz.question: According to the text, what do some fans like Georgia McAdam enjoy doing before a concert?
options: They like to buy last-minute tickets.
They like to know what the stage looks like.
They prefer to read books about the artist.
option_feedback: The text doesn't mention last-minute tickets for Georgia McAdam.
Yes, Georgia McAdam likes to be prepared and know details like the stage design.

grammar.explanation: The passive voice is used when the focus is on the action or the receiver of the action, rather than the performer. It is formed with a form of the verb 'to be' (e.g., 'is,' 'are,' 'was,' 'were,' 'been,' 'being') and the past participle of the main verb. For example, in the sentence 'key moments from her show were quickly discussed widely online,' the focus is on the 'key moments' and the action 'discussed,' rather than who did the discussing.
grammar.example_quote: Recently, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo began her Unraveled tour, and key moments from her show were quickly discussed widely online.

lesson.overview: Social media profoundly impacts the live concert experience by disseminating "big moments from headline acts" and revealing show details long before many fans attend, leading to divided opinions and artist responses.
lesson.topic: The impact of social media on live music experiences and audience expectations.

grammar.explanation: Reduced relative clauses provide a more concise way to give extra information about a noun. They often omit the relative pronoun (e.g., 'who', 'which', 'that') and a form of 'be' (e.g., 'is', 'are', 'was', 'were'). For example, 'Anyone [who is] found breaking the rules will be escorted out' becomes 'Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out.' The participle ('found' or '-ing' form) directly modifies the noun, making the sentence more efficient.
grammar.example_quote: Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out.

quiz.question: What is the primary way social media is affecting the live concert experience, according to the article?
options: It is causing artists to perform fewer shows.
It is revealing significant details about shows before many fans attend them.
It is increasing ticket prices for popular tours.
option_feedback: The article does not suggest that social media is leading artists to perform fewer shows; instead, it focuses on content sharing. This option is not supported by the text.

Correct. The article consistently highlights how social media platforms are used to share set lists, stage designs, and other "big moments from headline acts" before many fans get to experience them live.
The article discusses the financial cost for fans but does not link social media directly to an increase in ticket prices. This is an unsupported inference.

quiz.question: Aurélia Collins' efforts to "trick her algorithm" are an example of what, in the context of avoiding spoilers?
options: A common method for artists to promote their tours.
An attempt to gain early access to concert details.
"Extreme measures" taken to maintain the element of surprise.
option_feedback: Trick her algorithm is a fan's strategy, not an artist's promotional method. This option misinterprets the context and agency.
Aurélia Collins is trying to avoid details, not gain early access. This option contradicts her stated goal in the article.

Correct. The article states that some fans, like Collins, are taking "extreme measures" to preserve the element of surprise, which includes actively managing their social media feeds to filter out spoiler content.

quiz.question: How does Georgia McAdam's perspective on concert spoilers differ from Aurélia Collins's?
options: McAdam believes spoilers reduce the financial value of a ticket.
McAdam sees spoilers as exciting "teasers" rather than experience-diminishers.
McAdam thinks artists should actively encourage spoiler sharing.
option_feedback: The article does not mention McAdam discussing the financial value of tickets. Her focus is on the enjoyment aspect of spoilers.

Correct. McAdam is described as someone who "claims she loves them" and "sees online spoilers more as 'teasers' that do not diminish the thrill of the real thing." This directly contrasts with Collins's disappointment.
While McAdam enjoys spoilers, the article does not state she believes artists should actively encourage their sharing. This is an overstatement of her viewpoint.

quiz.question: When the article states that Olivia Rodrigo's tour surprises have been "dissected online," what does "dissected" most closely imply?
options: The surprises were hidden or kept secret.
The surprises were thoroughly analyzed and discussed in detail by fans.
The surprises were altered or changed by online viewers.
option_feedback: "Dissected" implies examination, not concealment. The opposite is true, as the surprises were revealed and discussed.
Correct. To "dissect" something means to analyze it in minute detail, which, in this context, refers to fans meticulously breaking down and discussing every aspect of the tour's surprises online.
The term "dissected" refers to analysis, not modification. Fans discuss what they saw, they do not change the actual surprises.

quiz.question: Which of the following sentences uses a reduced relative clause, similar to "Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out"?
options: The fan who had bought tickets early was excited for the show.
Security, alerted by the commotion, quickly intervened.
The artist's manager, who is known for strict policies, issued a statement.
option_feedback: This sentence uses a full relative clause: "who had bought tickets early." A reduced clause would omit "who had."
Correct. "Alerted by the commotion" is a reduced relative clause, meaning "Security, [who was] alerted by the commotion, quickly intervened." This matches the structure in the example.
This sentence uses a full relative clause: "who is known for strict policies." A reduced clause would omit "who is."

quiz.question: What can be inferred about artists' motivations for "switching up" their sets and incorporating "bespoke outfits"?
options: They are trying to reduce production costs.
They aim to avoid negative fan feedback about predictable shows.
They seek to maintain novelty and generate continued media buzz.
option_feedback: Customizing outfits and varying sets would likely increase, not reduce, production costs. This inference is incorrect.
While avoiding negative feedback might be a minor factor, the article emphasizes the proactive goal of creating new content for social media and press. This is not the main motivation presented.

Correct. The article suggests artists like Taylor Swift and Sabrina Carpenter use "bespoke outfits" and "switching up" sets to ensure "they're staying in the press" and generating new, viral content, indicating a desire to maintain novelty and buzz.

quiz.question: What is Laura Snapes' advice for fans who genuinely wish to avoid concert spoilers?
options: Attend only opening night shows to experience surprises first.
Unfollow all artists' social media accounts.
Actively avoid absorbing any of the online culture related to shows.
option_feedback: While attending opening night might help, Snapes' advice is more general about online behavior, not specific to ticket purchasing strategy. This is not her core recommendation.
Snapes specifically advises against looking at TikTok and absorbing the culture, which is broader than just unfollowing artists. This option is too narrow.

Correct. Snapes explicitly states that if fans want to be surprised, they "have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture" by staying offline, emphasizing a comprehensive digital detox from show-related content.

quiz.question: When the article states some fans "lap up" the opportunity for a preview, what does it imply about their reaction to spoilers?
options: They grudgingly accept the spoilers as unavoidable.
They are indifferent to the spoilers, neither liking nor disliking them.
They enthusiastically welcome and consume the spoiler content.
option_feedback: "Lap up" suggests eagerness and enjoyment, not grudging acceptance. This option misinterprets the idiom.
"Lap up" conveys a strong positive reaction, not indifference. This option is incorrect.
Correct. To "lap up" something means to receive it with eagerness and enjoyment, implying that these fans actively seek out and appreciate the preview information provided by spoilers.

quiz.question: Aurélia Collins was "gutted" when a spoiler about Niall Horan slipped through. What does this reveal about her emotional state?
options: She felt a mild disappointment.
She was extremely disappointed and deeply upset.
She was angry at the artist for revealing the spoiler.
option_feedback: "Gutted" is a strong, informal adjective indicating profound disappointment, not a mild one. This option understates her feelings.

Correct. "Gutted" is an informal but powerful term indicating extreme disappointment and upset, reflecting the significant emotional impact the spoiler had on her, especially given her long-standing fandom.
While frustration might be present, the primary meaning of "gutted" refers to disappointment and upset about a personal loss or missed opportunity, not specifically anger at the artist.

Attendees must keep their phones in silent mode throughout the performance.
Phones and recording devices are entirely banned and must be locked in a pouch.

The article specifies a ban and locking away devices, not just putting them on silent mode. This option is incorrect.
Correct. The article explicitly states that Bridgers is "banning phones altogether," requiring attendees to "lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch" upon entry.

"One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."
"If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."
Phoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether.
Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out.

McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans.
But Collins says she's "not totally against it".
What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want.
But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds.
"I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script.
